o: The input is a sequence of letter+count pairs, possibly repeating letters. We must merge counts per letter and emit `letter+total` pairs in alphabetical order. E.g. "a3c9b2c1" merges the two c-counts into c10 and reorders to "a3b2c10". Length up to 6·10⁴ and counts up to 10⁴ mean merged counts fit easily in normal integers; a linear parse suffices.
k: Parse (letter, number) pairs; numbers may have multiple digits.
Accumulate totals in a 26-size array indexed by letter.
Emitting in alphabetical order automatically sorts the output.

a.i: A regex `([a-z])(\d+)` extracts every letter-count pair at once; sum counts into an array and join the nonzero entries. Concise and linear.
s: Concatenate letter and count for every nonzero entry a..z.
a.t: O(n) — each character is examined a constant number of times
a.sp: O(1) extra beyond the output (26 counters)

a.i: Walk the string with an index: read one letter, then consume the following digit run, converting it to an integer. Avoids regex overhead and language regex differences.
s: i = 0; while i < length: read letter at i, advance.
Consume consecutive digits, accumulating the numeric value.
Add to the letter's bucket, then emit buckets a..z.

w: Use the manual parse in interviews — it shows you control the scanning and avoids regex-per-language pitfalls. Watch for multi-digit counts (a common bug is reading only one digit) and remember merged counts can exceed 10⁴ (use 64-bit if paranoid; 26 letters × 6·10⁴/2 pairs is safe in 32-bit but long is safer). Follow-up: what if letters could repeat non-contiguously with huge counts — the same bucketing still works.
